stem: Best guess: which penalty rate is higher per month — failure to file or failure to pay?

choices.explanation: Failure to pay is 0.5% per month.

explanation: Failure to file is 5% per month; failure to pay is 0.5% per month.

stem: A taxpayer files on time but pays $6,000 of tax 3 months late. What is the failure-to-pay penalty?
A preparer takes an undisclosed position that lacks substantial authority, earning a $3,000 fee on the return. What is the §6694(a) penalty?

choices.explanation: That is less than 50% of the fee.

explanation: §6694(a): greater of $1,000 or 50% of income derived = max(1,000, 1,500) = **$1,500**.

stem: A return with $20,000 of tax due is filed 2 months late with no payment until filing and no reasonable cause. What are the total failure-to-file and failure-to-pay penalties?
explanation: Combined 5% per month when both apply: 5% × 2 × 20,000 = **$2,000**.

stem: For an individual, when is an understatement "substantial" for the accuracy-related penalty?

choices.text: When it exceeds 25% of gross income
Over the greater of 10% of tax or $5,000
choices.explanation: Correct. §6662(d): greater of 10% of the tax required to be shown or $5,000 (corporations have a different test).

explanation: §6662(d): greater of 10% of the tax required to be shown or $5,000 (corporations have a different test).

stem: What is the civil fraud penalty?

choices.explanation: There is no 100% civil fraud penalty.
Correct. §6663: 75% of the portion of the underpayment attributable to fraud.

explanation: §6663: 75% of the portion of the underpayment attributable to fraud.

stem: A position has substantial authority but isn't disclosed. What is the effect on the substantial-understatement penalty?

choices.text: The penalty applies because the position wasn't disclosed
choices.explanation: Substantial authority avoids the penalty without disclosure.

choices.text: That item is excluded from the understatement
choices.explanation: Correct. Substantial authority (without disclosure) or reasonable basis (with disclosure) reduces the understatement.

choices.text: The civil fraud penalty applies instead

explanation: Substantial authority (without disclosure) or reasonable basis (with disclosure) reduces the understatement.

stem: Which standard must be met for a position on a tax shelter item to avoid the substantial-understatement penalty?

choices.explanation: Not enough for tax shelter items.
Correct. Tax shelter and reportable transaction positions require a reasonable belief the treatment is more likely than not proper.
Not the federal penalty standard for shelters.

explanation: Tax shelter and reportable transaction positions require a reasonable belief the treatment is more likely than not proper.

stem: A preparer fails to sign a return and fails to provide the client a copy. Which section imposes the penalties?

choices.explanation: Correct. §6695 imposes per-failure penalties for procedural failures.

explanation: §6695 imposes per-failure penalties for procedural failures.

stem: A preparer recklessly disregards rules and regulations, earning a $4,000 fee. What is the §6694(b) penalty?

choices.explanation: That's 75% of the fee, but the minimum is $5,000.

explanation: §6694(b): greater of $5,000 or 75% of income derived = **$5,000**.

stem: How long must a preparer keep a copy of a return (or a list of taxpayers and returns prepared)?

choices.explanation: Correct. §6107: keep a copy or list for 3 years after the close of the return period.

explanation: §6107: keep a copy or list for 3 years after the close of the return period.

stem: A taxpayer obtains an extension to file until October 15 but pays the balance due on June 15. Which penalty applies?

choices.explanation: The return is timely under the extension.
Correct. An extension to file doesn't extend time to pay.

choices.text: Both failure to file and to pay

explanation: Payment is due by the original due date; the failure-to-pay penalty (plus interest) runs from April 15.

stem: Which penalty can't be avoided by showing reasonable cause?

choices.explanation: Reasonable cause and good faith can excuse it.
Correct. Fraud involves intent, which is inconsistent with reasonable cause.

explanation: Reasonable cause excuses many penalties but not fraud.

stem: Which person is a tax return preparer subject to the preparer penalty rules?

choices.text: A neighbor who prepares a return for free
choices.explanation: Preparing a return without compensation does not make a person a preparer.

choices.text: A clerk who only types the return
An employee preparing the employer's return
choices.explanation: An employee preparing the employer's own return is excluded.

choices.text: A paid bookkeeper preparing a Schedule C
choices.explanation: Correct. Preparing a substantial portion of a return for compensation makes the person a preparer.

explanation: Preparer: prepares all or a substantial portion of a return or refund claim for compensation.

stem: A U.S. citizen holds two foreign bank accounts. During 2025 the combined balance of the two accounts never exceeded $9,000 on any day. Is an FBAR required?

choices.explanation: Correct. The test is the aggregate value of all foreign accounts at any time during the year; it never exceeded $10,000.

choices.text: Yes; any foreign account requires one
choices.explanation: Filing is required only if the aggregate value exceeds $10,000 at some time during the year.
Form 8938 is a separate FATCA requirement with higher thresholds.

choices.text: No; FBARs are only for businesses
choices.explanation: Individuals with foreign accounts are covered.

explanation: FBAR: aggregate foreign account value over $10,000 at any time during the year; FinCEN Form 114.

stem: A preparer takes an unreasonable position on a return and earns a $3,000 fee. What is the §6694(a) penalty?

choices.explanation: The penalty is 50% of the fee.
Correct. The greater of $1,000 or 50% of the fee.
That is the willful penalty floor.

explanation: §6694(a): the penalty is the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the income derived from the return.

stem: A preparer sells clients' tax information to a marketing firm without consent. Which consequence applies?

choices.text: No penalty, if names are kept

explanation: §6713 (civil) and §7216 (criminal) penalize unauthorized disclosure or use of tax return information by preparers.

stem: What is the penalty for filing a frivolous tax return?
explanation: §6702 imposes a $5,000 penalty for a frivolous return or submission.

stem: A taxpayer's negligence causes a $10,000 underpayment. What is the accuracy-related penalty?
explanation: The §6662 accuracy-related penalty is 20% of the underpayment attributable to negligence or substantial understatement.

stem: An individual promoter helps prepare a document he knows will understate another person's tax. What is the §6701 penalty?

choices.explanation: Correct. $10,000 if it relates to a corporation.

explanation: §6701 imposes $1,000 for aiding and abetting an understatement ($10,000 for a corporation's tax).

stem: A taxpayer relied in good faith on a competent CPA's advice after giving complete information. The position failed. What defense to the accuracy penalty applies?

choices.explanation: Correct. Reliance on a competent adviser can qualify.

explanation: Reasonable reliance on competent professional advice, with full disclosure of facts, can establish reasonable cause.

stem: A refund claim overstates the refund by $5,000 without reasonable cause. What is the §6676 penalty?
explanation: §6676 imposes a 20% penalty on the excessive amount of an erroneous refund claim.

stem: A preparer takes a position that has a reasonable basis but not substantial authority. How can the preparer avoid the §6694(a) penalty?

choices.explanation: Correct. Disclosure plus reasonable basis suffices.

choices.text: Charge no fee for the return

explanation: For non-tax-shelter positions, a disclosed position with a reasonable basis avoids the §6694(a) penalty.
